description: A ring of bread crusted in sesame seeds, sold from street carts from before dawn and eaten on the way to work. Chewy, faintly sweet, and stale by afternoon, which is why vendors sell out and go home by noon.

name: Bougatsa
description: Semolina custard between sheets of phyllo, baked, then cut up with a scraper and dusted with sugar and cinnamon in front of you. There is a savory cheese version too. Breakfast, and best from a shop that makes nothing else.

name: Spanakopita
description: Spinach, feta, dill and scallion between layers of oiled phyllo, baked until the top shatters. Sold in bakeries by the slab all day. The good ones have far more greens than cheese and are never soggy underneath.

name: Horiatiki
description: Tomato, cucumber, onion, pepper, olives and a whole slab of feta with oregano and olive oil — the village salad, and no lettuce anywhere in it. The oil left in the bowl is meant to be finished with bread.

name: Fava
description: Yellow split peas cooked to a smooth puree, served warm with raw onion, capers, lemon and a pour of olive oil. Not made from fava beans, despite everything. The best comes from Santorini and is worth asking about.

name: Gigantes plaki
description: Large white beans baked slowly in tomato with dill and olive oil until they go creamy inside. Served warm or at room temperature as part of a mezze spread. Nothing about it is fast, and it is better the next day.

name: Saganaki
description: A slab of hard cheese floured and fried in a small pan until it blisters and browns, served with lemon squeezed over it while it is still sizzling. Order it before the rest of the food and eat it immediately.

name: Moussaka
description: Layers of eggplant, spiced lamb and potato under a thick béchamel, baked until the top sets and browns. The version everyone knows was standardized by a Greek chef trained in France in the 1920s. Better warm than hot.

name: Pastitsio
description: Tubular pasta with cinnamon-spiced meat sauce under béchamel, baked and cut into squares. The cinnamon is what makes it Greek rather than Italian. Family food and taverna food, and always cut with a straight edge.

name: Loukoumades
description: Small yeast doughnuts fried and drowned in honey syrup with cinnamon and walnuts, served hot by the dozen. Said to have been given to victors at the ancient games. Eat them fast, before the syrup soaks all the way in.

name: Galaktoboureko
description: Semolina custard baked in phyllo and soaked in lemon syrup while still hot, so the top stays crisp and the base goes sticky. Cut into squares. Sweeter and more solid than it looks, and impossible to eat delicately.

name: Melomakarona
description: Small oval cookies of olive oil, orange and semolina soaked in honey syrup and topped with crushed walnuts. Made at Christmas by the hundred. They keep for weeks, and the syrup gets deeper into them as they sit.

name: Frappé
description: Instant coffee whipped with water, sugar and ice into a thick foam, served in a tall glass with a straw. Invented by accident at a trade fair in 1957. Ordered by sweetness, and drunk over an hour, never quickly.

name: Simit
description: A ring of bread dipped in grape molasses and crusted in sesame, sold from red carts on every corner and from men carrying trays on their heads. Chewy and faintly bitter. Eaten for breakfast, with tea, standing up.

name: Balık ekmek
description: A grilled mackerel fillet stuffed into half a loaf with raw onion, lettuce and lemon, sold from boats and stalls at the Galata bridge. Simple to the point of being nothing, and one of the best things in the city.

name: Midye dolma
description: Mussels stuffed with spiced rice, steamed and sold from trays on the street, opened one at a time and handed over with lemon. You pay by how many shells pile up. A late-night thing, and eaten in quantity.

name: Lahmacun
description: A very thin round of dough spread with minced lamb, tomato and pepper and baked in seconds. Not a pizza — it is rolled around parsley and lemon and eaten by hand. Cheap enough to order two without thinking.

name: Pide
description: A boat of dough baked with cheese, egg or minced meat, the edges folded to hold the filling, cut into pieces with a rocking blade. Order it with kaşar cheese and a raw egg cracked into the middle.

name: Adana kebap
description: Hand-minced lamb pressed onto a wide flat skewer and grilled over charcoal, spiced with red pepper and served with grilled tomato, onion and flatbread that soaks up the fat. Named for the southern city, and properly hot.

name: İskender kebap
description: Sliced spit-roasted lamb laid over cubes of bread, drenched in tomato sauce and browned butter poured at the table, with yogurt on the side. Invented in Bursa in the 1860s and still made under that family's name.

name: Mantı
description: Tiny dumplings of spiced lamb, boiled and served under garlic yogurt with melted butter and dried mint and red pepper poured over. Small enough that forty fit on a spoon. The smaller they are, the better the cook.

name: Menemen
description: Eggs scrambled slowly into tomato, green pepper and onion until soft and loose, served in the pan with bread for scooping. Breakfast, and the subject of one permanent national argument about whether onion belongs in it.

name: Kumpir
description: A large baked potato split and mashed in its skin with butter and cheese, then loaded with whatever you point at — olives, corn, sausage, pickles, russian salad. From Ortaköy, and the toppings are the entire event.

name: Kokoreç
description: Lamb intestines wrapped around offal, grilled on a spit for hours, then chopped fine with oregano and pepper and stuffed into bread. Organ meat, and the thing Istanbul eats at 3 a.m. It smells better than it sounds.

name: Künefe
description: Shredded pastry layered around unsalted stretchy cheese, baked in syrup and served hot so the cheese pulls when you cut it. Sweet and salty at once, topped with pistachio. Order it the moment it is made, never reheated.

name: Baklava
description: Forty or more sheets of pastry, clarified butter and pistachio, baked and soaked in syrup. Sold by weight and by cut — ask for şöbiyet or fıstıklı. Real ones shatter rather than squash, and the pistachios should be green.

name: Dondurma
description: Ice cream thickened with mastic and wild orchid root, so it stretches, resists the spoon and melts slowly. Vendors make a performance of taking it away from you before handing it over. Chewy in a way ice cream should not be.

name: Türk kahvesi
description: Finely ground coffee simmered with sugar in a small pot and poured grounds and all, drunk in small sips until you reach the sludge. Ordered by sweetness, not size. Served with water and, if you are lucky, a fortune read after.

name: Ćevapi
description: Small fingers of minced beef and lamb grilled over charcoal and served in a soft flatbread with raw onion and kajmak, by the five or the ten. The Balkans argue endlessly about whose are best. Ordered by number, not by plate.

name: Pljeskavica
description: The same minced meat as ćevapi pressed into one enormous flat patty, grilled hard and served in bread with onion, kajmak and ajvar. Bigger than the plate it comes on. Serbia's answer to a burger, and older than one.

name: Karađorđeva šnicla
description: Veal rolled around kajmak, breaded and fried, then served with tartar sauce — a 1950s invention nicknamed the maiden's dream, for reasons that become obvious. Enormous, molten inside, and entirely unserious.

name: Burek
description: Coiled phyllo filled with meat, cheese or spinach, baked in a huge round pan and sold by weight, cut in wedges. Eaten for breakfast with yogurt to drink. Greasy in a way that is the point rather than a flaw.

name: Ajvar
description: Red peppers roasted, peeled and cooked down with eggplant and oil into a thick relish, made in enormous batches every autumn and jarred for winter. Every family insists theirs is correct. Eaten on bread with cheese.

name: Kajmak
description: A fresh dairy spread skimmed from scalded milk and left to ripen, somewhere between clotted cream and young cheese, salty and slightly sour. Put on bread, on meat, inside everything. Nothing else quite tastes like it.

name: Gibanica
description: Layers of phyllo torn and mixed with eggs and salty white cheese, baked until the top curls and browns and the middle stays custardy. Served warm at every celebration and every ordinary breakfast alike.

name: Šopska salata
description: Tomato, cucumber, onion and pepper under a heavy snow of grated white cheese. Named for a region straddling three borders, and claimed by all of them. The cheese should completely hide what is underneath.

name: Riblja čorba
description: A peppery freshwater fish soup, red with paprika, made from whatever the Danube and Sava gave up — carp, catfish, perch. Cooked in a kettle by the river. There is also a famous rock band named after it.

name: Pasulj
description: White beans slow-cooked with smoked ribs, paprika and bay until the broth thickens by itself. The everyday winter meal of the whole country, cooked in vast pots. Eaten with raw onion and bread, and better reheated.

name: Urnebes
description: A fierce spread of crumbled white cheese, garlic, hot paprika and oil, mashed into a rough paste — the name translates roughly as chaos or pandemonium. Served with grilled meat, and it will overpower anything near it.

name: Krempita
description: Two thin layers of pastry with several centimeters of set vanilla custard between them, cut into squares and dusted with sugar. Sold from bakery windows in a solid slab. Eat it with a fork; it does not survive being picked up.

name: Tulumba
description: Ridged batter piped into hot oil, fried until deep gold and then soaked in cold sugar syrup so it stays crisp outside and syrupy within. Sold from trays, by the piece. Ottoman by inheritance, and sweeter than it looks.

name: Rakija
description: Fruit brandy — plum most often, but quince, apricot and pear all exist — distilled at home in enormous quantity. Drunk before a meal rather than after, at room temperature, in small glasses. Everyone claims an uncle who makes it.

name: Mici
description: Skinless grilled sausages of beef and lamb with garlic, pepper and baking soda, which is what makes them springy. Served in a pile with mustard and bread, never a bun. Ordered by the piece and eaten with beer, outdoors.

name: Sarmale
description: Cabbage leaves — pickled, not fresh — rolled around pork and rice with dill, cooked slowly with smoked meat and served with polenta and sour cream. Smaller and sourer than the Hungarian version. Christmas, and every Sunday.

name: Mămăligă
description: Cornmeal cooked to a thick polenta and turned out in a mound, cut with a thread rather than a knife. Eaten with cheese, sour cream, or under stew. It replaced bread for centuries in the countryside, and often still does.

name: Ciorbă de burtă
description: Tripe soup, white with sour cream and egg yolk, sharpened with vinegar and garlic and served scaldingly hot. The national hangover cure. Order it with a small dish of hot peppers and use them, one bite at a time.

name: Ciorbă de perișoare
description: Meatball soup soured with fermented wheat bran, thick with vegetables and finished with lovage — an herb that tastes like celery multiplied. The sourness is the defining feature of Romanian soup, and it takes a moment.

name: Zacuscă
description: Roasted eggplant and peppers cooked down with onion and tomato into a dark spread, made in huge autumn batches and jarred for the year. Eaten cold on bread. Every family's is different and every one is defended.

name: Salată de vinete
description: Eggplant roasted over flame until the skin burns, then chopped with oil and onion into a smoky, loose paste — never blended smooth. Served cold with tomato on bread. The wood-smoke taste is the whole reason for it.

name: Covrigi
description: Soft bread rings crusted in salt, poppy or sesame, sold hot from windows in the street for small change. Closer to a soft pretzel than a bagel. Eaten walking, at any hour, and best from a window with a line.

name: Drob
description: A baked loaf of chopped lamb offal with herbs, egg and onion, wrapped in caul fat and served cold in slices at Easter. Somewhere between a terrine and a meatloaf. Organ meat, and much gentler than the description.

name: Plăcintă
description: Thin pastry folded around salty cheese, potato, cabbage or apple and pan-fried or baked. Sold from bakeries and roadside stands in a paper napkin. The savory cheese one, eaten hot, is the one to start with.

name: Papanași
description: Two fried curd cheese doughnuts, one large with a small one perched on top, buried in sour cream and sour cherry jam. Enormous, hot, and meant to be shared, though nobody actually does. Order it after almost nothing else.

name: Cozonac
description: A sweet braided loaf swirled with ground walnuts, cocoa and rum, baked for Easter and Christmas and eaten in thick slices for days after. Dense, faintly boozy, and better toasted once it is a day or two old.

name: Țuică
description: Plum spirit, drunk cold in a small glass before food rather than after, and usually made at home rather than bought. Stronger than it tastes going down. Refusing a second is understood; refusing the first is not.

name: Croissant
description: Laminated dough folded with butter dozens of times and baked until it shatters. A straight one is made with real butter and a curved one usually is not — that is the convention, and it holds. Buy it before nine and eat it plain.

name: Jambon-beurre
description: Ham and butter in a baguette and nothing else: no cheese, no salad, no mustard unless you ask. France eats over a billion a year. The whole thing rests on the bread and the butter being good.

name: Croque monsieur
description: Ham and cheese toasted with béchamel and more cheese on top, browned under a grill. Add a fried egg and it becomes a croque madame. Café food since 1910, and the test of whether a café bothers with its kitchen.

name: Steak frites
description: A thin cut of beef seared rare under a pat of herb butter, with a mound of thin fries and no vegetable in sight. Order it saignant and expect it rarer than you meant. The fries are usually refilled without asking.

name: Soupe à l'oignon
description: Onions cooked down for an hour until dark and sweet, in beef broth under a raft of bread and melted gruyère. Market workers ate it at dawn at the old central market. Winter only, if you want it to make sense.

name: Escargots
description: Snails baked in their shells under garlic, parsley and a great deal of butter, served in a dimpled dish with tongs and a narrow fork. The snail is a delivery system for the butter, and the bread finishes the job.

name: Steak tartare
description: Raw beef chopped by hand and mixed with capers, shallot, mustard and egg yolk, either at the table or in the kitchen. Chopped, never ground — that texture is the whole difference. Order it with fries.

name: Blanquette de veau
description: Veal poached gently with carrot and onion, the broth turned into a cream sauce with egg yolk and lemon. Nothing is browned at any stage, which is the actual definition. Served with rice, and quietly loved by everyone.

name: Andouillette
description: A sausage made from coarsely cut pig intestine, grilled and served with mustard. It smells strongly of what it is, and you will either find it magnificent or you will not. Look for the AAAAA mark; the association is real.

name: Falafel
description: Chickpea fritters in pita with eggplant, cabbage, hummus and hot sauce, sold in the Marais with a line down the street. Not French in origin and entirely Parisian in practice. Eaten walking, and dripping.

name: Huîtres
description: Oysters from Brittany and Normandy, eaten raw by the half dozen with rye bread, butter and lemon, in brasseries with a shellfish stall out front. Ask for the flat ones if you want the strong metallic kind.

name: Paris-Brest
description: A ring of choux pastry split and filled with praline cream, created in 1910 to mark a bicycle race and shaped like a wheel. Hazelnut-heavy and less sweet than it looks. Eaten with a fork, never with hands.

name: Éclair
description: Choux pastry piped long, filled with chocolate or coffee cream and glazed on top in the same flavor. The name means lightning, supposedly for how fast it goes. Judge a pâtisserie on whether the glaze is thin and clean.

name: Mille-feuille
description: Three sheets of caramelized puff pastry with pastry cream between, glazed and marbled on top. It is built to shatter and collapse the moment you cut it, which makes eating one gracefully impossible.

name: Kir
description: White wine with a measure of blackcurrant liqueur, named for a Burgundy priest and mayor who served it constantly. Ordered before dinner at a café table in the late afternoon. Kir royal swaps the wine for champagne.

name: Bouillabaisse
description: A fish stew of rockfish, saffron and fennel, served as two courses: the broth first with rouille and toast, the fish after. Fishermen made it from what they could not sell. The real thing is costly and ordered a day ahead.

name: Panisse
description: Chickpea flour cooked to a paste, set, cut into batons and fried until crisp outside and creamy within, then salted hard. Sold from stalls in the old fishing quarter. The local answer to a french fry, and older.

name: Pizza moitié-moitié
description: Half anchovy and half cheese on a thin base from a wood oven, sold from vans since Italian families arrived a century ago. Ask for half and half and you will be understood. Emmental rather than mozzarella, which is the local way.

name: Aïoli
description: Garlic pounded with olive oil into a stiff yellow mayonnaise, served with poached salt cod, boiled vegetables and eggs — a whole Friday meal named after its sauce. The garlic is fierce and is meant to be.

name: Soupe au pistou
description: Summer vegetable and bean soup with a spoon of basil, garlic and oil stirred in at the table rather than cooked into it. Related to pesto, without pine nuts. Made when the beans are fresh, in late July and August.

name: Tapenade
description: Black olives, capers, anchovy and oil pounded into a coarse paste — the name comes from the Provençal word for caper, not for olive. Spread on toast before dinner. It should taste more of caper than you expect.

name: Anchoïade
description: Salted anchovies mashed with garlic and olive oil into a strong warm dip for raw vegetables and bread. Fishermen's food, unapologetically salty. Served at the start of a meal with something cold to drink.

name: Supions frits
description: Tiny whole cuttlefish floured and flash-fried, with lemon and sometimes garlic and parsley thrown over. Eaten with fingers at harbor tables. Sweeter and more tender than squid, and gone within minutes of arriving.

name: Pieds paquets
description: Sheep tripe parcels stuffed with salt pork and garlic, tied by hand and braised with trotters in white wine and tomato for hours. Organ meat, slow and gelatinous, and a genuine local specialty. Order it at lunch.

name: Fougasse
description: Flat bread slashed into a leaf shape so there is as much crust as possible, baked with olives, anchovy or bacon worked into the dough. Torn apart rather than sliced. Provence's focaccia, drier and crustier.

name: Chichi frégi
description: A long ridged doughnut fried to order and rolled in sugar, sold on the seafront and out at the beach villages. Orange-flower scented and greasy in the correct way. Eat it hot, from the paper, with your hands.

name: Navettes
description: Hard, dry boat-shaped biscuits scented with orange flower, baked at the same bakery near the abbey since 1781 and blessed in February at Candlemas. Meant for dunking, and they keep for months.

name: Pastis
description: Anise spirit poured into a glass and cut with five parts cold water, which turns it cloudy yellow. Drunk slowly in the shade before lunch with a bowl of olives. Ordering it neat marks you out instantly.

name: Frites
description: Potatoes fried twice — once low to cook them, once hot to crisp them — in a paper cone from a friture, with a sauce chosen off a list of twenty. Belgium claims the invention and defends it. Mayonnaise, or ask for andalouse.

name: Moules-frites
description: Mussels steamed with white wine, celery and onion, arriving in the black pot they cooked in with fries alongside. Use an empty shell as tongs for the rest. In season from summer into winter, cheapest in autumn.

name: Carbonnade flamande
description: Beef stewed in dark Belgian beer with onions, a slice of mustard-spread bread laid on top to dissolve and thicken it. Sweeter and deeper than a wine stew. Served with fries, because everything is.

name: Stoemp
description: Potatoes mashed roughly with a vegetable — carrot, leek, endive, kale — and a great deal of butter, served with sausage or bacon. Working-class Brussels food. The vegetable changes with the season and nobody minds.

name: Waterzooi
description: Chicken or fish poached in broth with root vegetables and thickened with cream and egg yolk, landing between a soup and a stew. From Ghent, adopted here. Eaten with a spoon and a fork at the same time.

name: Chicons au gratin
description: Belgian endive wrapped in ham, covered in béchamel and cheese and baked until browned. The endive stays faintly bitter under all of it, which is the point. It is grown in the dark, in cellars, near this city.

name: Filet américain
description: Raw beef minced with capers, onion, mustard and egg yolk, spread thickly on bread or served with fries. Nothing American about it. Sold in every butcher shop and eaten at lunch without any ceremony at all.

name: Gaufre de Bruxelles
description: A light rectangular waffle with deep pockets, made from thin yeasted batter, crisp outside and hollow within, eaten warm with powdered sugar and nothing else. This is the one to eat with a knife and fork.

name: Boulets sauce lapin
description: Large pork and beef meatballs in a dark sweet-sour sauce built on regional syrup, with fries. There is no rabbit involved — the name comes from the man who invented it. Sticky, strange, and better than it sounds.

name: Gaufre de Liège
description: A dense, chewy waffle made from bread dough studded with pearl sugar that caramelizes on the iron into a crackling crust. Uneven-edged, eaten hot from a stand, and nothing like the Brussels kind.

name: Speculoos
description: Thin, hard spiced biscuits pressed in carved wooden molds, tasting of cinnamon, clove and brown sugar, served with coffee everywhere. Belgium exported the crushed spread version, but the biscuit came first.

name: Cuberdon
description: A cone-shaped sweet with a hard crust and thick raspberry syrup inside, sold from purple carts. It lasts about three weeks before the center crystallizes, which is why it never exported. Bite the tip and squeeze.

name: Pralines
description: Filled chocolates — ganache, praliné, caramel — invented in Brussels in 1912 when a pharmacist's son put filling inside a chocolate shell. Bought by weight in a numbered box, and best eaten within days.

name: Gueuze
description: A blend of young and old lambic beers fermented with wild yeast from the air of one valley, refermented in the bottle and sour enough to startle you. Served corked, like wine. Nothing else in beer tastes like it.

name: Haring
description: Raw herring cured lightly in salt, served with chopped onion and pickle and eaten by holding it up by the tail. The new season's fish arrives in June and is fattest then. Not fishy at all — sweet, soft and clean.

name: Broodje kroket
description: A deep-fried roll of thick beef ragout, breaded and hot enough to burn you, in a soft white bun with mustard. The bread does nothing but hold it. Sold from vending machine walls, which is genuinely the best way.

name: Bitterballen
description: Round versions of the same ragout, breaded and fried and served by the dozen with mustard beside beer. The standard order in a brown café at five in the afternoon. Wait two minutes or you will burn your mouth.

name: Patat oorlog
description: Fries with mayonnaise, spiced peanut sauce and raw onion piled on together — the name means war, for how it looks. The peanut sauce arrived through Indonesia and colonial history. Eaten with a small plastic fork.

name: Kibbeling
description: Chunks of cod in seasoned batter, deep-fried and served in a tray with garlic or tartar sauce from a market fish stall. Originally made from cheeks and offcuts. The best stalls fry to order and the line still moves fast.

name: Stamppot
description: Potatoes mashed with kale, endive or sauerkraut, with a smoked sausage pressed into the middle and a well of gravy. Winter food, eaten early in the evening. Every version has a name and a devoted constituency.

name: Erwtensoep
description: Split pea soup cooked with pork until a spoon will stand up in it, with smoked sausage sliced through. Also called snert. Traditionally eaten after skating on frozen canals, and only correct when genuinely thick.

name: Rijsttafel
description: A dozen or more small Indonesian dishes served at once around rice — satay, rendang, sambals, pickles, fried banana. Invented by Dutch colonists to display the range of Javanese cooking. A meal that takes hours.

name: Gouda
description: Cheese aged from a few weeks to several years, running from soft and mild to hard, crystalline and almost caramel. Ask for oud, the aged kind, and eat it with mustard. Market stalls will cut samples for you.

name: Poffertjes
description: Small spongy pancakes made with buckwheat and yeast, cooked in a dimpled pan and served under butter and powdered sugar by the dozen. Eaten hot at winter markets with a tiny fork. Lighter than pancakes should be.

name: Stroopwafel
description: Two thin waffle discs with caramel syrup between them, cut fresh off the iron at markets. Rest it over a hot drink so the steam softens the syrup before you eat it. That instruction is not optional.

name: Appeltaart
description: A tall apple cake with thick pastry and a cinnamon-heavy filling, wedged with whipped cream and eaten with coffee in the afternoon. Denser and less sweet than the American pie, and ordered by the slab.

name: Hagelslag
description: Chocolate sprinkles eaten on buttered bread at breakfast, by adults, entirely without embarrassment. The butter is what makes them stick. The supermarket aisle for this is longer than the one for cereal.

name: Oliebollen
description: Deep-fried dough balls with raisins, buried in powdered sugar, sold from trailers that appear in December and vanish in January. Eaten outdoors at New Year in the cold. Better than a doughnut, and gone by the 2nd.

name: Jenever
description: Juniper spirit aged in oak, the ancestor of gin, poured brimming into a tulip glass that you bend down to sip without lifting. Ordered beside a beer, a pairing called a headbutt. Ask for oude, the maltier kind.
